note: No official key is marked on the master. All answers were determined by me and verified with sympy; every correct answer is choice (a) in master order. Q7 is ambiguous (y_p is only fixed up to adding c sin 2x; key 3/8 is the pure polynomial solution). Q11 is non-unique (see its note). Q17 asks for the Jordan form, which is outside the syllabus.

qs.q: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the initial-value problem \[ xy'=3y+x^4\cos x,\quad y(2\pi)=0, \] then $\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)^3 y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=$
hints: This is a first-order linear equation.
Divide by $x$ to put it in the form $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ and find the integrating factor.
$\rho=e^{\int P\,dx}$ and $(\rho y)'=\rho Q$; then use the initial condition to find the constant.
qs.brief: $\rho=x^{-3}$: $x^{-3}y=\sin x$, so $y=x^3\sin x$ and the value is $1$.

qs.q: Let $F(x,y)=e$ be the solution of the initial-value problem \[ (\cos x+\ln y)\,dx+\left(\frac{x}{y}+e^{y}\right)dy=0,\quad y(0)=1. \] Then $F(0,2)$ equals to
hints: Check whether the equation is exact.
Compare $\partial M/\partial y$ with $\partial N/\partial x$, then integrate $M$ with respect to $x$ and fix the missing function of $y$ using $F_y=N$.
If $M_y=N_x$ then $F=\int M\,dx+g(y)$ with $F_y=N$, and the solution curves are $F(x,y)=C$.
steps: $F_y=\dfrac xy+g'(y)=\dfrac xy+e^y$, so $g=e^y$ and $F=\sin x+x\ln y+e^y$.
Check: $F(0,1)=e$, which matches the given constant $e$.

qs.q: By using Cramer's Rule to solve the system \[\begin{aligned} 5x_1+4x_2-2x_3&=4\\ 2x_1+3x_3&=2\\ 2x_1-x_2+x_3&=1 \end{aligned}\] then $x_3=$
hints: Cramer's Rule expresses each unknown as a ratio of two determinants.
Compute the determinant of the coefficient matrix, then the determinant of the matrix with the third column replaced by the right-hand side.
$x_i=\dfrac{\det A_i}{\det A}$, where $A_i$ is $A$ with column $i$ replaced by the constant vector, valid when $\det A\neq0$.

qs.q: Which of the following sets $s=\{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\}$ forms a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$?
hints: A subset is a subspace when it contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
Test the zero vector first, then look for a pair of vectors or a scalar that breaks closure; also ask what each condition really says.
A sum of squares of real numbers is zero only when each number is zero; the solution set of a homogeneous linear system is always a subspace.
steps: $x_1^2+x_2^2=0$ forces $x_1=x_2=0$, so the set is $\{(0,0,x_3)\}$, which contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under sums and scalar multiples: a subspace.
$x_2=1$: the zero vector has $x_2=0$, so it is not in the set.
qs.brief: $x_1^2+x_2^2=0$ means $x_1=x_2=0$: the set $\{(0,0,x_3)\}$ is a subspace.

qs.q: Let the solution space of the system \[\begin{aligned} x_1-4x_2-3x_3-7x_4&=0\\ 2x_1-x_2+x_3+7x_4&=0\\ x_1+2x_2+3x_3+11x_4&=0 \end{aligned}\] have the following vectors $u=(-1,-1,1,0)$ and $v=(a,b,0,1)$ as basis for the solution space. Then $b-a=$
hints: Both basis vectors must satisfy every equation of the homogeneous system.
Substitute $v=(a,b,0,1)$ into the equations, giving equations in $a$ and $b$ only.
A vector lies in the solution space of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ exactly when it satisfies every equation; two independent equations in two unknowns can be solved directly.
steps: Put $x_1=a$, $x_2=b$, $x_3=0$, $x_4=1$ in the first two equations.
From the first, $a=7+4b$; substituting gives $14+8b-b+7=0$, so $b=-3$ and $a=-5$.
qs.brief: Plug $v$ into the equations: $a-4b=7$, $2a-b=-7$ gives $a=-5$, $b=-3$, so $b-a=2$.

qs.q: The general solution of the differential equation \[ y'''+3y''-4y=0 \] is $y=$
hints: This is a linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients.
Write the characteristic equation and factor the cubic by finding a simple root first.
Substituting $y=e^{rx}$ gives the characteristic equation; a root $r$ of multiplicity $k$ gives the solutions $e^{rx},xe^{rx},\dots,x^{k-1}e^{rx}$.
steps: $r=1$ is a root, and dividing gives $(r-1)(r^2+4r+4)=(r-1)(r+2)^2=0$.

qs.q: If $y_p$ is a particular solution of the differential equation $y''+4y=3x^3$, with $y_p(0)=0$ then $y_p(-1)=$
hints: The right side is a polynomial, so use undetermined coefficients.
Try a general polynomial of the same degree as the right side, substitute, and match coefficients of each power of $x$.
For $ay''+by'+cy=P(x)$ with $c\neq0$, try a polynomial $y_p$ of the same degree as $P$ (no extra factor of $x$ is needed).
qs.note: Strictly, y_p(0)=0 does not fix y_p (one can add c sin 2x); the key 3/8 is the pure polynomial particular solution.

qs.q: If $y_p=\cos x\,\ln|\csc x+\cot x|+u_2\sin x$ is a particular solution of the differential equation $y''+y=\csc^2x$, then $u_2(x)=$
hints: This is variation of parameters with $y_1=\cos x$, $y_2=\sin x$.
Compute the Wronskian of $\cos x$ and $\sin x$, then the formula for $u_2'$.
steps: $u_2(x)=-\csc x$. As a check, $u_1'=-\sin x\csc^2x=-\csc x$, so $u_1=\ln|\csc x+\cot x|$, matching the given term.

qs.q: A basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$ which consists of eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}10&-8\\6&-4\end{bmatrix}$ is
hints: Find the eigenvalues, then an eigenvector for each.
Solve $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, then solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ for each eigenvalue.
Eigenvalues are roots of $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so they form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

qs.q: Suppose that a $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has the eigenvalues $\lambda_1=2$ and $\lambda_2=1$ and their corresponding eigenvectors $v_1=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$ and $v_2=\begin{bmatrix}3\\2\end{bmatrix}$, respectively. If $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}x&y\\z&w\end{bmatrix}$, then $x+y+z+w=$
hints: Diagonalization: $A=PDP^{-1}$ with the eigenvectors as columns of $P$.
Form $P$ and $D$, then compute $A^2=PD^2P^{-1}$.
If $A=PDP^{-1}$ then $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$, and for $P=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, $P^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$.

qs.q: Given that $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2&1\\2&0&1\\2&-2&3\end{bmatrix}$. If $A^{-1}=aA^2+bA+cI$, then $12(a+b+c)=$
hints: Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to relate $A^{-1}$ to powers of $A$.
Compute $\det(A-\lambda I)$, write the polynomial relation satisfied by $A$, and multiply by $A^{-1}$.
A square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial, and $A^{-1}$ exists when the constant term (which equals $\pm\det A$) is nonzero.
qs.note: Intended answer uses the characteristic-polynomial relation (Cayley-Hamilton, not in the syllabus). A also satisfies a degree-2 relation (A^2=5A-6I), so aA^2+bA+cI is not unique and 12(a+b+c)=4c+14/3 for free c; the key 10 corresponds to the characteristic-polynomial choice.

qs.q: The differential equation $x^{(4)}+6x''-3x'+x=\cos 3t$ can be transferred into a system of linear first-order differential equations of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\\x_4\end{bmatrix}'=A\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\\x_4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\\\cos 3t\end{bmatrix} \] where $A=$
hints: Convert a higher-order equation to a first-order system by naming each derivative.
Let $x_1=x$, $x_2=x'$, $x_3=x''$, $x_4=x'''$ and solve the equation for $x^{(4)}$.
With $x_1=x$, $x_2=x'$, $x_3=x''$, $x_4=x'''$: $x_1'=x_2$, $x_2'=x_3$, $x_3'=x_4$, and $x_4'=x^{(4)}$ is expressed from the equation.

qs.q: If $X=c_1\begin{bmatrix}2\\2\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{t}+c_2\begin{bmatrix}2\\0\\-1\end{bmatrix}e^{3t}+c_3\begin{bmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{5t}$ is the solution of the initial value problem $X'=\begin{bmatrix}3&-2&0\\-1&3&-2\\0&-1&3\end{bmatrix}X,\ X(0)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\2\\6\end{bmatrix}$, then $c_1^2+c_2^2=$
hints: Use the initial condition to get a linear system for $c_1,c_2,c_3$.
Set $t=0$ in the general solution, so every exponential becomes $1$, and solve the resulting $3\times3$ system.
At $t=0$: $X(0)=c_1\mathbf v_1+c_2\mathbf v_2+c_3\mathbf v_3$, a linear system with the eigenvectors as columns.
steps: Simplify: $c_1+c_2+c_3=0$, $c_1-c_3=1$, $c_1-c_2+c_3=6$. Subtracting the third from the first gives $2c_2=-6$, so $c_2=-3$; then $c_1+c_3=3$ and $c_1-c_3=1$ give $c_1=2$, $c_3=1$.

qs.q: The solution of $X'=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\3&4\end{bmatrix}X,\ X(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ at $t=\pi$ is equal to
hints: The eigenvalues of this matrix are complex.
Find a complex eigenvalue and eigenvector, then split the complex solution into real and imaginary parts.
For $\lambda=a+bi$ with eigenvector $\mathbf v=\mathbf p+i\mathbf q$, the real solutions are the real and imaginary parts of $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v=e^{at}(\cos bt+i\sin bt)(\mathbf p+i\mathbf q)$.

qs.q: If the general solution of $X'=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\3&-1\end{bmatrix}X$ is $X=c_1\begin{bmatrix}1\\a\end{bmatrix}e^{-2t}+c_2\begin{bmatrix}b\\1\end{bmatrix}e^{\lambda t}$, then $a+b+\lambda=$
hints: Each term of the solution is an eigenvalue and eigenvector pair.
Find the eigenvalues from the characteristic equation, then an eigenvector for each; scale to match the given shapes.
$X=\sum c_ie^{\lambda_it}\mathbf v_i$ where $(A-\lambda_iI)\mathbf v_i=\mathbf 0$.

qs.q: The general solution of $X'=\begin{bmatrix}1&-3\\3&7\end{bmatrix}X$ is $X=$
hints: Look at the eigenvalues; a repeated eigenvalue with too few eigenvectors needs a generalized eigenvector.
Find the eigenvalue and its eigenvector $\mathbf v$, then solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf w=\mathbf v$.
For a defective repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$: $\mathbf x_1=\mathbf ve^{\lambda t}$ and $\mathbf x_2=(\mathbf vt+\mathbf w)e^{\lambda t}$, where $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf w=\mathbf v$.
steps: $A-4I=\begin{bmatrix}-3&-3\\3&3\end{bmatrix}$: eigenvectors satisfy $v_1+v_2=0$, so take $\mathbf v=(-3,3)$ (only one independent eigenvector).
Solve $(A-4I)\mathbf w=\mathbf v$: $-3w_1-3w_2=-3$, so $w_1+w_2=1$; take $\mathbf w=(1,0)$.

qs.q: The characteristic equation of a matrix $A$ is $(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)^3=0$, where we have only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=-2$. The Jordan normal form of $A$ is
hints: The number of independent eigenvectors for an eigenvalue equals the number of Jordan blocks for it.
The eigenvalue $-2$ has multiplicity $3$ but only $2$ eigenvectors, so split $3$ into $2$ block sizes.

Each Jordan block has the eigenvalue on the diagonal and $1$ above it; block sizes for one eigenvalue add up to its algebraic multiplicity, and the number of blocks equals the number of independent eigenvectors.
steps: $\lambda=1$ is simple, so it gives a $1\times1$ block.
$\lambda=-2$ has multiplicity $3$ and $2$ eigenvectors, so it has $2$ Jordan blocks with total size $3$.
The only possibility is one block of size $2$ and one of size $1$.
So the form has $1$ and a single $-2$ as $1\times1$ blocks, and a $2\times2$ block $\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\0&-2\end{bmatrix}$ for the other $-2$'s, with no other off-diagonal entries.
qs.brief: Two blocks for $\lambda=-2$ (sizes $2$ and $1$) plus a $1\times1$ block for $\lambda=1$.
qs.note: Jordan normal form is outside the Math 208 syllabus (listed as not taught); kept because it is on the exam. Solved by block counting.

qs.q: A possible fundamental matrix for the system $X'=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-4&2\end{bmatrix}X$ is $\Phi(t)=$
hints: A fundamental matrix has linearly independent solutions as its columns.
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and form each column as $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$.
If $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ then $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ solves $X'=AX$; the columns $e^{\lambda_it}\mathbf v_i$ form $\Phi(t)$.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3&4\\0&2&6\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}$. If $e^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}e^{2t}&f(t)&h(t)\\0&e^{2t}&6te^{2t}\\0&0&e^{2t}\end{bmatrix}$, then $f(1)+h(1)=$ (Hint: Consider $A=D+B$, where $B$ is a nilpotent matrix)
hints: Split $A$ into a diagonal part and a nilpotent part that commute.
Take $D=2I$ and $B=A-2I$; compute the powers of $B$ until they vanish.
If $D$ and $B$ commute, $e^{(D+B)t}=e^{Dt}e^{Bt}$, and for nilpotent $B$ with $B^3=0$: $e^{Bt}=I+Bt+\dfrac{B^2t^2}{2}$.

qs.q: Let $F(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$ and $e^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}1+2t&-4t\\t&1-2t\end{bmatrix}$. A particular solution for the system $X'=AX+F(t)$ with $X_p(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ will satisfy $X_p(1)=$
hints: This is variation of parameters for systems, with a given matrix exponential as the fundamental matrix.
Use the formula with $\Phi(t)=e^{At}$, whose inverse is $e^{-At}$, and the zero initial condition.
$X_p(t)=e^{At}\int_0^te^{-As}F(s)\,ds$ (this satisfies $X_p(0)=\mathbf 0$), with $e^{-As}$ obtained by replacing $t$ by $-s$ in $e^{At}$.
